noticias.resumen: My Decoder guest today is Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, and we’re discussing the new wave of consumer-friendly AI agents. If you’ve been paying attention to this space, you know AI enthusiasts have been using agents for a minute now — homebrew OpenClaw setups led to a surge in Mac Mini sales earlier […]
noticias.contenido: My Decoder guest today is Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, and we’re discussing the new wave of consumer-friendly AI agents. If you’ve been paying attention to this space, you know AI enthusiasts have been using agents for a minute now — homebrew OpenClaw setups led to a surge in Mac Mini sales earlier this year. But the launch of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and xAI’s Grok bot has brought easy to use agents to millions. Muse and Dots have had the highest-profile product launches, and they’re fascinating to pit against each other. Both Meta and OpenAI have decided to pitch these agents to mainstream users and businesses in the form of cute, animated mascots . Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . These can do everything from the boring — restaurant reservations and inbox triage — to more sophisticated tasks. In OpenAI’s cases, the company is even offering “specialist” Dots for marketing, legal work, and accounting. Muse, notably, is free, while Dots are not. So you’ll hear Hayden and me get into why Meta, which still doesn’t have a frontier model of its own, might have a meaningful edge here because it’s so much better at making and distributing consumer products. There’s also a huge Decoder -style tension wrapped up in the agent race: a conversation about what AI is good at today, what it still can’t do, and then the privacy and security implications of handing over your credit card information, your email inbox, and other sensitive hard drive data to an AI that might be able to do things for you without even requiring an app or a phone in your hand. That might be the future of all computing, but it’s not at all clear if most people want to hand over the data to make it happen. Okay: The Verge ’s Hayden Field on Muse, Dots, and trusting AI agents. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Hayden Field, you’re the senior AI reporter here at The Verge . Welcome back to Decoder . Thanks so much. I’m excited to talk to you. This time there isn’t any wild interpersonal drama. No one’s feelings have been hurt. I would say Elon Musk tried to hurt some feelings and didn’t get there. Alexandr Wang from Meta has maybe been taking some shots, but none of the Real Housewives stuff we usually end up talking about when you’re on the show. It’s been a bit of a pause in the soap opera antics for now, which I’m really grateful for. Yeah, just some good old-fashioned product competition in the marketplace. Let’s see who wins and loses, and maybe everything will kill us all in the end. But, for now, cute mascots. There’s a lot going on. Let’s start at the start. Hayden, you were at OpenAI DevDay in San Francisco. The company announced Dots, which is their new agent platform with a cute mascot. That happened just a few weeks after Meta Connect, at which the company was all in on Muse, their agent platform with an adorable mascot. Tell us about the state of the industry right now. Everyone’s very excited about agents. What’s going on? It’s funny to me because I’ve been covering agents for so long. I remember that in 2022, it was the year of ideation — that’s what tech leaders called it, referring to agents. They were just ideating. They were thinking about what it could look like. There were a lot of references to Jarvis from the Marvel Universe. They called 2023 the year of deployment: “Let’s try things, let’s deploy and learn more about what’s failing.” Which meant pretty much all of them were failing at the time. Then we had 2024 and 2025. They didn’t have any names for those years, but agents were still pretty bad, as we saw. 2026 seems, to me, like the year of the beginnings of actually useful AI agents for the consumer, like always-on autonomous agents. Obviously, OpenAI was the start of all of this. But what’s interesting to me is that one man, Peter Steinberger, was able to create an actually useful AI agent for the consumer with OpenClaw — an always-on tool, despite its privacy flaws. It had a lot of privacy and security issues. But it was an agent that was useful enough that people still wanted to use it anyway and try to find ways around these privacy issues that it was having. That inspired these companies to say, “If one man can do this over the course of one weekend, we’ve really been slacking. We have to get it together.” OpenAI hired that guy, and now we have Dots. Meta, of course, was working on its own version of this and put it out sooner with Muse. They’re basically both always-on, autonomous AI agents that these companies are peddling as a way to be your personal assistant in a lot of ways. The idea is to use them for booking flights, booking dinner reservations, buying gifts for people, but not only that. Some of them, Dots in particular, are kind of going further to be your work personal assistant and we’ll get into that in a minute. But this is where OpenAI and Meta are warring right now. They’re trying to present these two AI agents as a little bit different from each other, even though they’re essentially the same. Just broadly speaking, to define some terms, we’re gonna keep saying “agent,” and what we mean here is an AI model wrapped in a harness that lets it use a computer. Right. The way that I describe AI agents usually is an AI tool that can complete multi-step complex tasks on your behalf without you hand-holding it the whole time. I was a personal assistant in one of my first jobs in New York, so I would’ve gotten fired if every time my boss asked me to book a flight for her, I said, “What time? Also, what’s your SkyMiles number? Also, what’s your loyalty number again, for this other thing? Oh, do you want me to try to get you first class?” They want you to have common sense and just book the flight. This is what they’re pitching these AI agents as — things that can work on their own mental kind of scratchpad in the background and not ask you every single time there’s a step. They can complete multi-step processes in the background, doing their own reasoning, and then present you with a completed task. That’s the big idea. Just to say it clearly, both Muse and Dots come out of the OpenClaw lineage, which is a technical approach to building an agent, right? There are a lot of different ways you might be able to accomplish “It’ll remember your SkyMiles number and book you a flight.” But the way everyone’s going at it now is the idea of a harness around a model. That was the big innovation in OpenClaw, and the computer OpenClaw was using was often your own Mac Mini on your own network using a wide-open browser with your own data, which is where a lot of their security problems came from. It’s the same model with Muse, only it’s a little Linux computer that Meta’s giving you in the cloud. It’s the same model with Dots, although the way ChatGPT is set up with Codex is very complicated, and that computer could be in a lot of different places. But this notion that what you really need is a computer with a browser and some harness is gonna direct a model to do a bunch of stuff for you using that computer, that’s what we’ve landed on today, and it just seems to be the default winning model. Right. Are all of these things just riffs on OpenClaw? Are they the same as OpenClaw? You could say that. They’re different technically. Meta keeps saying, “We did build this from scratch, but it was inspired by OpenClaw.” There are a lot of similarities there , but they did say that they built it from scratch. Then, of course, OpenAI hired the creator of OpenClaw, so there’s probably a lot of similarities there as well for Dots. The reason I wanted to stay there for one second is that I think it’s important to identify the fundamental technical approach that is happening with these agents, because there’s a lot of different ways it could have gone, and the whole industry has picked this approach. What you need is a web browser, a harness, and a model that can go use that web browser. What’s really interesting to me is that Meta has done a really good job on top of that fundamental model of making a cute consumer product. Meta is good at consumer products. Obviously, Instagram and Facebook and the rest are undeniably good consumer products. People really like them. For all of Meta’s failings in VR, I always thought the Meta Quest has been a great consumer product. You take it out of the box, it helps you use it, you can have fun with it right away. Whereas Dots seems like it’s kind of made for software engineers, but you can also plan a wedding in it. I’m wondering if that’s how you see it. That one is an enterprise product with a little consumer gloss on it, and then Meta obviously is just a dead-ahead consumer product. What’s different here is that OpenAI needs money a lot more than Meta needs money. The products are honestly pretty similar, it seems like. The difference is that OpenAI is marketing it to be an enterprise-friendly product a lot more than Meta is. Muse is just a consumer-facing product. Meta is happy with that. The goal is to make Muse as easy to use as humanly possible. One-tap downloading, just putting it in your face literally everywhere. Even when I went to my Instagram profile the other day, there was a pop-up for using Muse. They’re trying to make it free, accessible, and super easy to broaden the audience. They want anyone to be able to just use it with one click and get used to it. They’re trying to flood the market with AI agents and make it normal and have their own ChatGPT moment, if you will, for AI agents. They want Muse to be that. Now, with OpenAI, they’re still marketing it as a consumer-facing product. When you’re using ChatGPT, if you have the right subscription, it’s right there. It says, “Use your Dot to do this, that, and the other.” They really want you to go for it as a consumer, as long as you’re paying. This is for their $100 to $200 a month subscription tier, unlike Meta. That’s why there’s a huge difference here. For OpenAI, it seems like they don’t have the money to just front-load all of this and say, “Use it for free. No problem. We’ll catch up with you later.” OpenAI wants this to be a money-making product, and that’s why they’re marketing it to the enterprise. They talked a lot about privacy to try to set it apart from Meta’s Muse. They talked a lot about what you could do with this as a knowledge worker, whether you worked in marketing, graphic design, software engineering, product, and tons of different industries. They gave examples of how you could use this as an assistant, as a coworker. Sam Altman even referred to it as like a “chief of staff.” He didn’t want it to be just an assistant. He wanted it to be your chief of staff. Something else that I thought was interesting is that Sam Altman seemed to subtly dig at Meta on stage a few times during DevDay. One of the times he said, “Look, I don’t want this to be just something that’s used to book flights or plan things with friends and look at your calendar. I want this to go beyond that and to really do knowledge worker tasks, things that you in your industry would need a niche assistant to perform.” That’s why they also introduced specialist Dots that are good at marketing, legal analysis, and things like that. They’re really going for the enterprise angle here, but I think it’s also because they need money ahead of their IPO, obviously. Yeah, the revenue piece — that it’s only for paid customers at their higher tiers — is really interesting. OpenAI’s tiers are very confusing, but it’s $100 and up, and that’s just going to keep a lot of people from using Dots at first. The flip side of that is OpenAI does have a lot of customers who are paying them a lot of money, and if they can get those customers to start using Dots, then those customers will be on their agent platforms and maybe you will get some lock-in. You’ve given those agents a lot of data. They’re part of your workflows, and that might solve the problem I think we’ve seen all the frontier labs have, where a new model comes out and it’s slightly better than the competitor model, and everyone switches for six months, and the next new model comes out and everyone switches back. Is there some thought that these agent platforms create lock-in — create actual loyalty on top of just the models being better? Yes. They’re basically hoping that they can build a moat with their users for these things. If Meta and Google already have super easy integrations with all of each company’s existing tools and services, they can easily keep you there. For example, I have an Apple iPhone, but I use almost exclusively Google apps. So if Google had an AI agent that I was using every day, it would be a little tough for me to switch. That’s what they’re hoping for here. Meta is hoping that they can get you so into the Muse ecosystem that it would be tough for you to switch, and maybe one day you do have to pay. With OpenAI, they’re trying to get you locked into their ecosystem right away. Even though you have to pay up front, they’re thinking, “We have integrations with almost every tool and service. Maybe it’s not as good as the company that owns that tool and service, but we have the variety and the breadth.” They’re going for quantity here. One of their employees told me that. They said, “Maybe our Gmail integration, for example, isn’t gonna be as good as Google’s, but we have a Gmail integration and an Outlook integration and X, Y, and Z.” They’re going for just the power of choice and the fact that power users will hopefully stay in this moat. It’s funny, you mentioned Google. Google announced an agent called Gemini Spark. We should mention that SpaceXAI, the very coherent company that everyone understands, has an agent called Grok Bot, which it is promoting heavily. People seem to like it. It was built by the Cursor team, which SpaceX acquired. There’s a lot of this going around, but it seems like Meta really got there first with a consumer product that people could understand. Obviously, Grok Bot and Dots are much more enterprise-focused, coding-focused. Why was Meta able to get there first? From all my reporting on Meta, they’ve been behind in AI for a while, and Mark Zuckerberg basically said, “We’ve got to lock in and make a product that people are gonna use on our platforms.” Alexandr Wang apparently was more looking to create a frontier model that was gonna compete with the other leading frontier models. He says, “We have to think long-term. We have to think superintelligence.” But Zuckerberg says, “No, we gotta think cold hard cash, as in getting people to use stuff on our own platform.” Where they met in the middle was an AI agent that people would use on the Meta platforms, but that still represented a huge step forward, they hoped, for AI systems and what they could do in the everyday world. This is a fascinating dynamic in that Meta still doesn’t have a frontier model. I don’t think anyone at Meta is claiming that the Muse Spark model competes at the frontier of GPT-6, but their product is better, and certainly they have a massive distribution advantage. They don’t have to pay for advertising on Meta platforms, and OpenAI does, and certainly they have a consumer design advantage. Meta is just better at consumer products. Does that change how you feel about the dynamics of competition in AI at all? For so long, it’s just been about the capabilities at the frontier, but now it’s a little bit about marketing. It’s a little bit about product design. You don’t have the best model, but you made a consumer agent product and you connected it to giving everybody a computer in the cloud, so now it can actually do things for you, and its frontier capability is actually not the important thing. It’s its capability. I think the more money and power you have at one of these companies, the more get mentally farther away from what the average consumer wants. Let’s say the average consumer does want an AI agent, which many of them don’t, as we know. But let’s say they do. If they do, they’re going to want it to be free or cheap, and they are going to want it to be safe to use without creeping them out too much. They’re willing to deal with a little bit of creepiness in order for it to be free, but not too much. Meta’s Muse has made headlines about some of its privacy issues that have gotten a little bit above that comfort level for some users. That’s probably why OpenAI at DevDay made a lot of remarks about privacy and the importance of that, especially if they’re trying to court enterprise users with their AI agents. Right now these companies, especially Meta, are trying to flood the market and create a mass market appeal for this stuff. Similar to how ChatGPT became the default AI chatbot, Meta wants to be that for AI agents, and they feel very hungry about it. They want to create a ChatGPT moment for this technology by making Muse the default for the general public. There’s something really interesting about the idea that a less-than-frontier model wrapped in a better product is actually going to be the success story here versus a bleeding-edge frontier model that is a little bit harder to use. There’s some dynamic in there that is the history of all consumer tech products, right? The worst product that’s easier to use often wins, but we haven’t seen that yet in AI. Right. That’s really important to note here because not everyone needs the bleeding-edge frontier model. Software engineers do. They see a huge difference with coding prowess from one model to another, and that’s why they’re always switching. But the general public, if they’re using an AI agent, as long as it’s useful, they’re good. However, not many of them are useful yet. We’re still testing Muse and Dots ourselves. For Muse, I saw a couple anecdotes yesterday that it had a big flop for a day or so. People felt like the capabilities got a lot worse. For Dots, the jury’s still out. We’re still testing it. It depends on what industry you’re in and what you’re really using this stuff for. That’s why OpenAI is going for enterprise, because it makes money and they’re confident that their agent is going to be more and more helpful in these niche industries. That’s also why they launched specialist Dots, because as we know, the more specialized, niche info you feed into an agent or model, the better it’s going to perform. They don’t want to have that imbued into every single general-purpose agent. It’s just too pricey and too compute heavy, so they say, “You know what? Let’s launch these specialists.” I feel like you and I talk about consumer versus enterprise adoption of AI every time you’re on this show, and here it seems very important to note that OpenAI asking people to pay a lot of money and asking people to use it primarily in enterprise context is gonna overcome what I think of as the brittleness problem, just because enterprise and business customers have a lot of economic incentives to figure out how to make something work. If I’m paying OpenAI $100 a month, and I’m using the marketing Dot to solve some marketing automation, and it doesn’t work the first time, it is very likely I will try again. Because if I get it right, then maybe I’ve saved some money or some time in my business that is really good, and I’ll do it again, and eventually that will lead to more revenue for me, the business owner. What I know about consumers is that the first time it doesn’t work, they just walk away. They have no incentive to try again to overcome frustration or brokenness. We’ve seen this happen with Muse now a few times. I’ve seen it myself with Muse, where it pops open a browser and tries to do something, and it runs into a brick wall or a CAPTCHA or Amazon blocking it , and it says, “I can’t do it that way. Do you want me to try another way?” And I say, “Whatever. I was just screwing around, and I’m never gonna try it again.” These are very different markets. OpenAI has vacillated between wanting to be the big consumer company and knowing that the revenue is in enterprise. Do you see any focus in Dots, or do you see that personality shift back and forth in the product itself? So far, I’m a little bit more impressed with Dots than Muse, just because everyone was impressed with Muse right away, but since then there have been a lot of ups and downs, plus the privacy stuff has been really interesting. Even the fact that it’s building profiles on your family and closest friends . Meta has never been a super trusted company. None of these companies are very trusted, but Meta has made a lot of missteps with user privacy. Dots seems to be a little bit more helpful to me right now, but I’m still testing, I’m not fully sure yet. I need to run through all my typical things that I do to compare. Everyone has their own short list of tasks. Right now, for example, I’m trying to create an album of my bachelorette photos, and it’s been unbelievably hard to get any agent to try to do that, so I say, “I’ll just do it myself.” But that’s a pretty easy thing to do. Once again, how useful are these things for our everyday lives, really? We’ll see. They’ve gotten a lot better, I will say, over the past few years. I’ve been shocked at how slow they’ve been moving, but they have gotten better. Dots is a little bit more impressive to me right now, but we’ll see. I have Muse plugged into my Instagram because I don’t worry about sharing my metadata with Meta in the way that I worry about maybe everything else, but they already have my Instagram. So I have Muse plugged into my Instagram, and it’s just doing all kinds of stuff. It surfaces interesting comments that I should reply to on Instagram posts. It tracks follower counts. It suggests things I should make videos about. It has horrible ideas. Muse is absolutely convinced I should make a video almost every single day about obscure Australian tech regulation. I don’t know why it has this idea. I’m up on it now. I’m deep in the weeds on Australian tech regulation just because I see it every morning. But there’s something about all that that still feels like work to me. I’ve just assigned it work, and then it tells me what work I should do, and I haven’t found some great consumer use for it yet. Organizing my photos is a consumer use. It kind of still rhymes with work, but it at least is not actually work. Have you found a great consumer use for these yet? Not one that works, and that’s the problem. I’ll try to have it do something for me for my wedding or for my personal life, and they haven’t been good yet. That’s why I’m still kind of running through and testing these, because so far it’s always interesting factually when they can do something, but I haven’t been able to trust them end-to-end with something that I really, really need done. It reminds me of the analogy for AI agents. People always say right now they’re a bad intern, and what you want them to be is a really good assistant, or in Sam Altman’s words, a really good chief of staff. They’re no longer a bad intern, but I think maybe they’re an okay or “eh” assistant. I don’t think they’ve reached the point of being a really, really good assistant yet, but I still need to run through the rest of my tests to see. It seems they’re not super consistent yet, which is something that you need in a really good assistant. That ties into trust. You’ve mentioned trust several times now. I’m only willing to give Muse access to, again, the Meta platforms that Meta already has access to. I can’t worry too much about that. I’ve given it access to my spam Gmail, so it is collecting a lot of ideas about my spam Gmail. But Meta really wants my credit cards. It wants to go through all of my credit card receipts. This is one of the suggestions in Muse. One of its suggestions is, “Let me log into your credit cards and I’ll cancel streaming services you’re not using,” or, “I’ll negotiate your Verizon bill for you.” I am absolutely not ready to give Meta one ounce of data more than it already has. This feels like a big issue for every agent. There’s an argument that you should give Meta all that data, one, because they already have it, and two, because they’re a big company that you could sue if they get something wrong. Whereas if I gave all of my data to OpenClaw, it’s just my own fault if it gets leaked. If I gave all my data to one of the hot startups like Instinct and they go out of business, well, that’s just the end of that. How do you feel about this? Do you feel comfortable giving your data to Meta? Do you think people should do that? No, I don’t feel comfortable, and I also don’t think that the general person does either. If I’ve seen one thing in a lot of the comments on our Meta story that we published in the last couple weeks, it’s that people don’t trust Meta at all. I have to say, why would they? But I don’t think that you should trust OpenAI a lot more either. It’s everyone’s own comfort level that they have to abide by. Some people are going to get a lot out of this stuff. Some people may say, “I don’t care if they use my data as long as they are negotiating down my bill accurately or canceling streaming services that I wouldn’t be canceling on my own, so they’re saving me money. It’s fine.” But one, are they actually gonna be able to do that accurately? Some people have said no. And as we know, when you release data like this, you can’t undo it. I always think about that old example of the insurance company that theoretically buys data on what’s in your fridge and maybe charges you a higher premium if you’re buying too much beer and not enough bananas. That’s just a theoretical example, but that’s the type of thing that can happen. People should operate with caution, abide by their own comfort levels, but I’m certainly not comfortable yet giving my personal data to Muse. I don’t know that I’m comfortable giving access to that level. I don’t even know if I’m comfortable putting Muse on my Mac. Apple just recently changed how apps can access the disk on Macs because Muse was so aggressive about reading data. In particular, Jason Aten is a columnist at Inc. and it read his notifications off the disk because he had just given it a permission and he didn’t realize Muse would take that permission and go do something else with it. This is a lot of spiraling concerns. You’re going to have a little robot that can use your computer for you, whether that computer is in the cloud or whether it’s on your desktop, and you might not know what it’s doing. That ties directly into the fact that OpenAI often doesn’t know what its agents are doing, and that has led to catastrophic security problems across this industry. Can you connect those dots? Is your own little agent doing your travel booking the same kind of threat as OpenAI’s agents hacking Hugging Face? I don’t think it’s the same type of threat, but it’s definitely something that you should keep in mind when you’re using this stuff. I link that back to the Facebook Marketplace debacle that we saw with Meta’s Muse. To recap, basically a Muse agent, without someone’s knowledge, invited a potential buyer of this item that this guy was selling to his house, and said, “He’s available now.” He wasn’t home, and then the potential buyer said, “Are you here? I’m trying to get the item.” And then Muse responded on his behalf, “Yeah, I’m here,” and then he just never came down because obviously he wasn’t home. There was a lot of drama going on there. Some people said, “He did give Muse access to his Facebook Marketplace, so he should have known this could happen.” A lot of people don’t read all the fine print when they check “yes” to one of these things. There’s a lot there. There’s a lot to unpack in that gray area. But the point is that people should just be a little wary before checking “yes” to every possible thing that these agents want to access, like you said about the credit cards or disk access. It’s easy to just check “yes” and say, “Whatever, I’ll figure it out later,” but people should be reading the fine print or even use AI to read the fine print. That is one great use of AI. Get it to read the terms and ask it, “What are the worst possible things that could happen here? Lay it out for me.” Those are things that people should keep in mind before they move forward. And then as for the so-called rogue AI agents that have been hacking other companies and stuff from these labs, it’s just important to notice that if they can’t control some of their most powerful unreleased AI models, how well are they going to be able to control your data or your agent? Sam Altman said during DevDay that you have a ton of control over your Dot. He said that there were a lot of “if this, then that” rules you can create. There are a lot of specific stipulations that you could make in terms of permissions of what your Dot could and couldn’t do. So that did give people some peace. But as we’ve seen, these labs and these large tech companies have had a lot of missteps about hacking other companies, and more are coming out every single week, more news items about these cyberattacks. We’ve seen Meta have one. We’ve seen OpenAI have a ton. We’ve seen Anthropic have a ton. This is all just stuff to keep in mind. One cool thing that I saw someone do was to name their AI agent after the CEO that runs that company and then see how much data you feel comfortable giving it. If you want to do that, I think that’s a great idea, and then it just kind of makes you think twice. If you’re saying, “Sam Altman, go through my email and see what needs to be deleted,” maybe you still feel comfortable with that, but maybe it makes you think twice and think, “You know what? Maybe I’ll give it access to my spam email only,” like you said. This ties into the fact that all these things are really cute. Muse is cute. The mascot Jolly is very cute . Alexandr Wang has been waging a relentless campaign on X to make it not only cute but sexy , which you can feel any way you want about that. But he keeps tweeting memes of the mascot with a butt. Dots are obviously very cute. They come in different shapes and sizes. There’s something here where you’re not quite anthropomorphizing the agent, but you’re making it a character and you’re giving it personality. That connects to the idea that you’ve called AI Tamagotchis , where eventually we’re going to have a little hardware device with your little cute mascot on it, you’ll talk to that instead of your phone, and this is the big promise this whole industry has been working toward for forever. They’re gonna replace your phone and the entire paradigm of the App Store with AI agents that are going and using computers for you. Do you think that any of these products are a meaningful step towards that? They’re just one building block along the journey of the goal that they’re chasing here. I haven’t heard of anyone that’s using Muse or Dots so far for everything. It’s not Jarvis from Iron Man , despite how much these CEOs want both these products to be that. They are a meaningful step, but as for the cuteness, I think one of the most important points here is that they are intentionally disarming. These tools are made to be cute so you don’t find them threatening, or you find them decidedly non-threatening. They’re cute. They’re there to help you. It’s a response to the AI populism backlash. It’s saying, “This isn’t going to hurt you or do anything bad. It’s just a cute little thing with eyes, or a sexy little thing with eyes,” whatever. Just to be clear, I do not think it’s sexy. I think Alexandr Wang has been relentlessly trying to make it sexy. [Laughs] No, I also do not think they’re sexy, but I will say Elon Musk has been trying so hard to make all agents and chatbots sexy, so I’m sure it’s not far off for someone to think that. But whether the AI agents of the future are cute or sexy, it’s going to be equally disarming. [Laughs] That’s the whole spectrum? The spectrum, the cute-sexy graph. It’s going to be really disturbing to see when we go more along that graph. The point is they’re supposed to be disarming and that people should really think twice before giving too much of their data, or just pick and choose what you’re comfortable sharing. Like how you did with the spam email versus your regular email, or saying “no” to giving it your credit card. These are both new products, so just see how the cookie crumbles before you decide to give everything over. We’re already seeing a bunch of changes week to week with how people are using Muse or what they’re upset about, so see how it shakes out. The last piece I want to talk about is just how any of this makes money. You and I have talked many times about the bubbly nature of the AI economy. Zuckerberg has said his plan is for Muse to take a cut of transactions on the backend. Zuck has given everybody a little Linux computer in the cloud with 8GB of RAM. Obviously, he’s given away tons of free tokens. He does not have to pay advertising costs. He can just put Muse across all of his platforms. To the extent that Meta is a well-oiled machine, the amount of Muse promotion that is happening across Meta platforms instantly is kind of incredible to see. They just turned it on. I saw an ad during NFL games this weekend from Muse. They are spending money to promote this. They’re giving it away for free. They’re giving the tokens away for free. And then somewhere at the end of this, they’re gonna say to merchants, “This person was shopping for shoes. Muse brought them to your doorstep. You’re gonna pay for this customer to buy shoes from you.” I don’t know any merchants that are excited about this, and it certainly feels like merchants that pay Meta more money would be preferred merchants, and that means that not only do I have an assistant or chief of staff, I have a bribable chief of staff. Like, I have a corrupt butler. Is that what you want? That is a great term for it, a corrupt butler. That is not what I want, and I don’t think many people do. It’s just crazy to me that we’ve gotten so far from what people really want, which is they want to trust a recommendation and they don’t wanna be scammed, you know? The leaders in AI don’t think about how certain things have been mirrored in other industries. Think about when people were paying for reviews for their businesses, or paying to delete reviews for their businesses. There was a huge uproar. Or influencers getting paid to recommend products without disclosing that it was an ad. We then saw the rise of micro-influencers, who were more valuable for a while because they were seen as more trustworthy. They didn’t have that many followers, so the things they recommended must be really good, right? And then we saw the, “Oh, okay, well, there’s #ad, but also they only said they were going to recommend things they really believe in, so it’s okay that it’s an ad.” There are these mental gymnastics that people have to do to figure out what is really a trustworthy recommendation these days. What is going to convince people that an AI recommendation is trustworthy, if it can be bought? That’s something these companies are really gonna have to reckon with. The ChatGPT ads blowback was huge , and OpenAI had to say, “It’s going to be a clearly disclosed ad underneath your query, not influencing your query.” If you’re using Muse to shop and it’s an undisclosed potential Meta customer that you’re being redirected to, to buy those shoes instead of these other ones, I feel like so many people aren’t going to use these tools to shop. I get it on the Meta side. I understand why they would think about monetization that way. They’re a consumer company. This is a consumer product. They know the second they charge even a dollar for it, the uptake will drop precipitously, so they have to keep it free, and then a bunch of people are going to want to shop and go buy a new iPhone cable. At the end of the day, it’s all just the same Amazon garbage anyway, so whatever. Then they can run an auction on the backend to say, “Who wants to pay us, Meta, the most for the privilege of selling an unbranded USB-C cable to this customer?” They’ll run some auction, and that will, in its way, just sort of maximize the money that gets turned around. That is broadly how advertising works today. That’s how the Google Search results page worked until recently, because now it’s full of AI and they’re probably going to do the same thing. Meta can do that because they already have a giant advertising business that prints money. They can give away a consumer product. Mark Zuckerberg has shown he’s willing to blow money trying to win a market like he did with Reality Labs for years and years and years, and they can just run it till it works. OpenAI, even at $100 a month, is probably not making money on those customers. In fact, I think we know they’re not making money on those customers. They don’t have any monetization, and when they do try to turn on ads, people get mad at them. How can OpenAI keep up with Zuck? Only via enterprise. That’s why they are pushing this so hard. We saw a ton of enterprise discussion, demo videos, customer feedback, and tons of other stuff at DevDay, and that’s why they’re pushing this so hard — because they can’t keep up with Zuck on the consumer front. They just can’t. This is the part where, when people ask if it’s a bubble, I just find myself wondering how much of the economy does Zuck have to win in order to give away millions upon millions of free tokens and 8GB of RAM to everyone in the cloud? Because that is just an expensive thing to give to everyone. How many percentage points of every shoe sale in America do you need to take to fund it? And the answer is it feels like a lot. That’s huge here and something to remember because we already saw Zuck crash and burn with the metaverse stuff, and he does not want to be embarrassed again. So how long is this going to go on, and how are they going to fund it in a real way on the backend, like what you were saying? It’s just a little bit tough to imagine. Luckily, Meta has a ton of money, and they can redirect stuff from other departments, which we’ve already seen them do a lot. It will be interesting to see how this fares on the next couple of quarterly earnings calls — to see how much money is being funneled into this and how much it is making, if any. And how many people are using it. Because they’ve announced it at the top of the App Store, but our own David Pierce has written an entire story about how being number one in the App Store doesn’t mean much . It’s sustained success that actually means something. It reminds me of when I was in college and Uber and Lyft, or maybe it was just Uber honestly, were new and VC-backed, so it was around $4 to call an Uber anytime you wanted to go out or down to the bars or anything. They got everyone using it, and then they got everyone hooked, and then they had to up the prices. That happens. That’s a tale as old as time with VC-backed products. So what I’m wondering is if AI agents are really going to become like that. Are they going to get enough users and enough like shoe sales on the backend that this is gonna be a really viable business model? Or is it just going to kind of be a potentially big bet that they switch away from later? That’s what some Meta employees that I spoke with in our Meta piece told me. They said they expect this to be something that they’re putting out, trying to make a big deal of, and then they may evolve away from it later on, or at least partly. We’ll see how that goes. If your bet is that the future of computing is talking to a little agent, it certainly seems like Meta has gotten farther along that path than anyone else. But we’ll see. OpenAI has hardware designed by Jony Ive that will theoretically come out. It is certain that Google and Apple and all the rest will respond at some point. Hayden, this was great. Thank you so much for being on Decoder once again. Thanks so much. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

noticias.titulo: Restituyeron a una familia francesa un violín robado por los nazis en 1940
noticias.resumen: Con el avance de las tropas alemanas, Gabriel Girondelot huyó de la casa donde vivía con su familia a unas horas de París para refugiarse en el sur del país; en diciembre de 2024, el instrumento reapareció en una subasta
noticias.contenido: Transcurrieron alrededor de 80 años para que un violín Caressa que había sido sustraído por militares alemanes durante la ocupación de Francia volviera a la familia de Gabriel Girondelot , que había denunciado su robo en 1945. “Es la primera restitución pública en Francia de un instrumento musical desde los años 1960”, dijo Pascale Bernheim , cofundadora de la asociación Musique et Spoliations , que llevó a cabo las investigaciones. Restaurado por la Maison Vatelot-Rampal, el violín Caressa volvió a sonar en la Maison Paul Beuscher, en París, bajo los dedos de Sarah Dayan , acompañada al piano por David Kadouch. “Este momento musical devuelve el instrumento a la vida para la que fue concebido, tras más de ocho décadas de ausencia”, señalaron desde la asociación ante la consulta de LA NACION . Originalmente, el violín fue fabricado en 1905 en el taller “Caressa & Français”, con el número 152 . La documentación disponible no permite establecer con certeza quién fue su primer propietario. Sin embargo, las investigaciones permitieron determinar que Gabriel Girondelot tenía en su poder dos violines de esa casa , y que al menos uno de ellos había pertenecido a su cuñado Eugène Paul Choubry , quien obtuvo en 1913 el primer premio de violín del Conservatorio de París. La asociación consideró posible que ese instrumento haya pertenecido a Choubry, aunque aclaró que se trata de una hipótesis que no pudo ser demostrada con papeles. Choubry murió en combate durante la Primera Guerra Mundial, en 1917 , y era hermano de Madeleine Choubry, esposa de Girondelot. Este último, notario y coleccionista de antigüedades, conservó varios violines en propiedades de la familia en la región de la Marne. El robo del instrumento Con el avance de las tropas alemanas en Francia a mediados de junio de 1940, Girondelot huyó con su familia de la región de la Marne para refugiarse en el sur del país. Parte de sus bienes había quedado almacenada en dos castillos, entre ellos varios instrumentos musicales. Según la declaración que realizó después de la guerra, cinco violines fueron retirados por soldados alemanes el 15 de junio de 1940 . En 1945, tras regresar a la región, Girondelot declaró el robo de los cinco instrumentos ante las autoridades , entre ellos el violín Caressa de 1905 número 152. El instrumento quedó registrado posteriormente en el Répertoire des biens spoliés en France durant la guerre 1939-1945 —el inventario de bienes expoliados durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial—, con Girondelot como propietario. Según la investigación llevada adelante tras la guerra, los cinco violines conservados en el castillo de Maisons-en-Champagne fueron sustraídos el 15 de junio de 1940. Los soldados alemanes los cargaron en un camión junto con otros objetos de uso cotidiano, como bicicletas y una máquina de coser. Dos testigos, los esposos Richer —jardineros del castillo—, habrían presenciado su sustracción, según pudo saber este diario. Girondelot murió en 1954 sin tener más noticias del instrumento hasta que, en diciembre de 2024, el violín reapareció en una subasta de instrumentos de cuerda frotada en Vichy, en el centro de Francia . Las autoridades detectaron que el instrumento coincidía con uno de los declarados desaparecidos en 1945 y suspendieron inmediatamente la venta. Las características del violín y, en particular, el número 152 permitieron avanzar en su identificación. Posteriormente, las investigaciones del Ministerio de Cultura y del Museo de la Música confirmaron que se trataba del instrumento buscado. Este miércoles, y luego de ser restaurado por los lutieres de La Casa Vatelot-Rampal , el centenario violín regresó a los herederos de la familia de Girondelot . “Es emocionante”, afirmó Clémence Houdart, bisnieta de Girondelot, contenta de que hechos así vuelvan “a crear vínculos familiares”. “En el marco del famoso Einsatzstab ERR del Reichsleiter Rosenberg, un equipo especializado llamado Sonderstab Musik (Comando Musical) fue enviado a Francia ya en agosto de 1940 para recoger instrumentos musicales, así como partituras manuscritas importantes y otros documentos relacionados con el repertorio alemán”, explica la asociación Musique et Spoliations en su página web. “Tras la guerra, la búsqueda de instrumentos saqueados no despertó en Francia el mismo entusiasmo oficial que la búsqueda de obras de arte perdidas. Así, los instrumentos declarados saqueados por sus legítimos propietarios aparecen en el censo titulado Répertoire des biens spoliés (Índice de Bienes Saqueados) bajo la anotación ‘solicitud denegada, 13 de junio de 1961’”, prosiguió la entidad.

noticias.titulo: El incómodo acto de Trump en Texas: protestas, interrupciones y encuestas complicadas
noticias.resumen: El presidente viajó por tercera vez en menos de un mes al estado históricamente republicano donde ahora podrían ganar los demócratas
noticias.contenido: SAN ANTONIO.– El presidente Donald Trump regresó el miércoles a Texas para movilizar a los votantes republicanos en apoyo del candidato al Senado Ken Paxton , en un mitin interrumpido repetidamente por manifestantes, en un momento de creciente presión electoral para el Partido Republicano en uno de sus principales bastiones. Ante una multitud en el Freeman Coliseum de San Antonio, Trump dedicó buena parte de su discurso a respaldar a Paxton , a quien definió como “ quizás el mejor fiscal general de los Estados Unidos” , y atacó reiteradamente a su rival demócrata, James Talarico . Fue la tercera visita de Trump a Texas en menos de un mes , una señal de la importancia que los republicanos atribuyen a conservar el control del estado en las elecciones de noviembre. Texas no elige a un senador demócrata desde 1988 y Trump ganó allí las presidenciales de 2024 por casi 14 puntos. Sin embargo, la contienda por el Senado se volvió competitiva. Una encuesta de The New York Times /Siena College publicada el fin de semana mostró a Talarico con 51% de intención de voto entre los votantes probables , frente a 45% para Paxton . El escenario también está condicionado por el desgaste de Trump . Una encuesta de Reuters /Ipsos realizada esta semana situó su aprobación en 32% , mientras que entre los votantes registrados los demócratas aventajaban a los republicanos por 44% a 37% en preferencias para el Congreso . En este contexto, los republicanos ya destinaron más de 300 millones de dólares a las elecciones en Texas. Trump respaldó a Paxton en las primarias republicanas, en las que derrotó al senador en ejercicio John Cornyn, y ahora busca trasladar su capital político al candidato. La relación entre ambos, sin embargo, no siempre fue fluida. La semana pasada Trump había calificado a Paxton de “un verdadero fastidio a veces”, mientras que este miércoles lo presentó como “un hombre fantástico” . El presidente evitó referirse durante el acto a una grabación filtrada recientemente en la que Paxton expresaba preocupación por la guerra en Irán , el aumento de los precios del combustible y la conducción de su campaña por operadores políticos de Washington. TRUMP DANCE IN THE LONE STAR STATE — THANK YOU, TEXAS! pic.twitter.com/seaVzL3ZZ3 — Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 8, 2026 Tras sus ya clásicos y llamativos pasos de baile, Trump concentró sus ataques en Talarico, a quien criticó por sus posiciones sobre distintos asuntos y llamó repetidamente “Tala-freako” (una combinación del apellido con la palabra “freak”, que indica que una persona es anormal). También cuestionó su postura sobre la pena de muerte, un tema especialmente relevante en Texas, que históricamente concentra el mayor número de ejecuciones en Estados Unidos. “Texas será destruida casi instantáneamente si Talafreako entra” , aseguró el mandatario. “La gente de Texas no va a dejar que espectáculos freaks débiles, cobardes, haters y promotores de la ideología transgénero destruyan todo lo que hemos construido”, agregó. Trump: "Texas will be almost instantaneously destroyed if Talafreako gets in" pic.twitter.com/AvEB9jTlWs — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 7, 2026 Interrupciones Las protestas fueron otra de las características visibles del mitin. Al menos una docena de manifestantes interrumpieron al presidente y varios fueron retirados por la policía . Uno de ellos fue agredido físicamente por un simpatizante de Trump de edad avanzada cuando intentaba abandonar el recinto, según imágenes difundidas en redes sociales. En otro episodio, Trump se apartó brevemente del micrófono cuando un manifestante pareció acercarse al escenario. Después de que fuera retirado, dijo: “Se va a casa con su madre” , y agregó: “Pero lo que no sabe es que su madre votó por Trump” . Los simpatizantes respondieron a las interrupciones con cánticos de “U-S-A”, mientras Trump calificaba a los manifestantes de “pagados” y afirmaba, sin aportar pruebas, que eran financiados por “los enemigos de nuestra nación”. A crowd member assaults a protester after the protester heckles Trump in Texas. pic.twitter.com/M5AkTxYENk — Molly Ploofkins (@Mollyploofkins) October 7, 2026 “Protegemos nuestro país” El presidente también aprovechó el acto para referirse a sus recientes comentarios sobre la posibilidad de que Irán atacara ciudades estadounidenses como Los Ángeles o San Diego . Trump insistió en que Estados Unidos no permitirá que eso ocurra y defendió al mismo tiempo el elevado costo de los combustibles como consecuencia de la guerra. “No vamos a permitir que eso suceda. Protegemos nuestras ciudades. Protegemos nuestro país”. La guerra con Irán y el aumento del costo de vida se convirtieron en asuntos centrales de la campaña para las elecciones de mitad de mandato, en las que los republicanos se juegan el control de ambas cámaras del Congreso. La situación política también afecta al gobernador republicano Greg Abbott, que busca un cuarto mandato y no asistió al mitin de Trump . En cambio, estaba previsto que participara en la inauguración de un hospital a unos 530 kilómetros de San Antonio. Abbott enfrenta una contienda más competitiva de lo habitual contra la demócrata Gina Hinojosa , en un nuevo frente para los republicanos en un estado que durante años fue considerado un bastión conservador prácticamente inexpugnable. La carrera al Senado concentra, de todos modos, la mayor atención nacional. Talarico ha logrado recaudar importantes sumas de dinero y convertir la elección en una disputa competitiva , mientras Paxton intenta mantener para los republicanos un escaño que ocupan desde hace décadas. Paxton apareció en el escenario hacia el final del acto y agradeció el respaldo del presidente . “Estoy muy agradecido de que esté aquí”, dijo. Agencias AP y AFP

noticias.titulo: Magnific tiene un plan para acabar con el "slop" de la IA
noticias.resumen: Un fantasma recorre las calles de todas las ciudades del mundo: el fantasma de la IA . Caminando por Madrid, bastan apenas unos minutos para encontrar multitud de carteles generados con inteligencia artificial. La mayoría son menús de bares y restaurantes que, durante años, se habían mantenido estáticos ante los elevados costes de sustitución. Lo que un día suponía contratar a un diseñador e invertir altas cantidades de dinero en una carta hoy requiere un puñado de segundos . La IA, así, ha tomado las calles a la fuerza. Sucede que este drástico cambio en el paisaje urbano viene acompañado de…
noticias.contenido: Un fantasma recorre las calles de todas las ciudades del mundo: el fantasma de la IA . Caminando por Madrid, bastan apenas unos minutos para encontrar multitud de carteles generados con inteligencia artificial. La mayoría son menús de bares y restaurantes que, durante años, se habían mantenido estáticos ante los elevados costes de sustitución. Lo que un día suponía contratar a un diseñador e invertir altas cantidades de dinero en una carta hoy requiere un puñado de segundos . La IA, así, ha tomado las calles a la fuerza. Sucede que este drástico cambio en el paisaje urbano viene acompañado de un problema: todos los carteles son iguales. Podemos elevar un sinfín de quejas ante el gremio de los diseñadores, pero no podemos negarles la virtud de la originalidad. Más o menos acertados, sus carteles se diferenciaban los unos de los otros en función de la estética del establecimiento o de las preferencias del hostelero. La IA ha arramplado con cualquier forma de distinción. Las tonalidades doradas, las tipografías serpenteantes y cursivas, los contrastes agudos. Todo luce exactamente igual . Joaquín Cuenca, CEO de Magnific, la mayor empresa de IA española y una de las plataformas de IA más utilizadas en todo el mundo, no es ajeno a este problema. Durante la presentación de Magnific One , la nueva herramienta lanzada hoy por la compañía , resaltaba la ubicuidad de "la estética IA". Hay un subtono, un carácter, una forma de crear que permite reconocer las imágenes generadas por IA al instante. Todas las dificultades que tenemos para reconocer textos generados por Claude se convierten en facilidades para identificar carteles hechos con ChatGPT. En Xataka La española Magnific lanza One: una IA que toma por ti las decisiones de composición, luz, cámara y estilo ¿Cómo solucionamos el problema? La pregunta solo es trivial si uno considera que la IA es una moda pasajera, algo a duras penas defendible en pleno 2026. El abaratamiento de las capacidades creativas hace inviable un futuro donde miles y miles de comercios y negocios se abstengan de utilizar IA. La mayoría de ellos, como sucede ahora, recurrirán a versiones gratuitas y a modelos más bien modestos. El resultado, a pie de calle o en Internet, será un mundo dominado estéticamente por la IA. ¿Es ese un buen futuro? Como hemos comentado en alguna edición de Caras B , la industria tecnológica ha encontrado en el "gusto" , o más bien en el "buen gusto" , una vía de escape hacia el futuro hiperdemocrático al que la IA nos conduce a toda velocidad. Cuando todo el mundo sea capaz de generar un texto o una imagen a través de un modelo, la única vía de distinción será tener un ojo exquisito, un estilo llamativo, una manera de disponerse frente al mundo que señale indefectiblemente nuestro talento, nuestra humanidad. Nuestro "buen gusto", en suma. "Durante 16 años, el gusto ha sido nuestra responsabilidad como creativos. Magnific One lo lleva a la IA como un estándar Magnific sobre la tecnología en la que funciona (…) Llévale una idea y te devuelve direcciones que nunca habrías encontrado solo", nos explicaba Cuenca en un encuentro con los medios durante la mañana de ayer. One se presenta como una capa que afina los modelos a modo de "dirección creativa" donde las decisiones de composición, colorización y óptica se modulan bajo el criterio de la compañía. "Somos creativos y creemos que eso implica una responsabilidad con la cultura visual que compartimos", añaden. La pelea por definir el "gusto" Este movimiento no es exclusivo de Magnific. Mark Zuckerberg, Jensen Huang y otros CEO de empresas tecnológicas llevan ya varios años obsesionados con señalar su distinción a través del arquetipo del "buen gusto" por excelencia: la ropa . La conversación sobre el "gusto" se ha insertado en el corazón de Silicon Valley, ecosistema cultural caracterizado tiempo atrás por los vaqueros slim , las zapatillas deportivas, las camisetas básicas y una dejadez consciente por aquello que la cultura burguesa consideraba presentable o admirable. Es un cambio cultural significativo. Así, es plausible pensar que en el futuro consumiremos productos a dos velocidades: por un lado, aquellos adscribibles a la IA, generados de forma industrial y sin mayor consideración por la estética; por otro, aquellos adscribibles a los creadores humanos, deudores de siglos de arte y pensamiento, producidos cuidadosamente de forma artesanal y ofrecidos a un mercado boutique de consumidores conscientes , preocupados por el gusto. O al menos eso querremos creer quienes optemos por lo "humano" frente a lo "artificial". En Xataka Freepik, ganador del Premio Xataka especial a la mejor empresa tecnológica española de 2025: de banco de imágenes a rival de Adobe Desde este punto de vista, es comprensible que las empresas de IA pivoten hacia un futuro donde la distinción sea parte de su identidad corporativa. Magnific quiere combatir el slop mediante capas que afinen sus imágenes a través de conocimiento humano y creativo, que destaquen en el mar de imágenes clónicas en el que se ha convertido Internet. Anthropic quiere diferenciarse de otras empresas mediante tonos marfil y tipografías con serifa , recuperadas para la causa como símbolo del clasicismo y de la alta cultura en una era de turboindustrialización de la creatividad. Colgar un menú generado por IA en la puerta de tu restaurante comunicará cocina batallera y poco esmero por la comida; colgar un menú diseñado por un joven ilustrador señalará una aspiración por las cosas bien hechas y la gastronomía elevada. ¿Quién querrás ser? Como bien explica Antonio Ortiz en este artículo , sucede que la cuestión del "gusto" lleva muchas décadas disputada. La dicotomía que aquí presento ya existía en los tiempos en los que Pierre Bourdieu escribió 'La distinción' , solo que aplicada a cuestiones más vetustas, como la música clásica. El gusto, como estamos observando en tiempo real de la mano de Silicon Valley, no es un conjunto de criterios objetivos flotando en el espacio, allí dispuestos para quien desee adquirirlos. Es más bien el resultado de procesos sociales donde una élite —sea cultural, sea social, sea política, sea económica— decide marcar terreno y las condiciones de acceso a su posición. La capacidad de apreciar las sinfonías y la alta literatura, explicaba Bourdieu, no era innata sino heredada, y funcionaba como barrera de entrada para las clases menos educadas. Si no las conocías o sabías apreciarlas, significaba que no formabas parte de la élite. Esta visión desdeña la construcción del gusto. Es defendible que la "alta cultura" sea nada más que una construcción artificial sostenida sobre los anhelos elitistas de un grupo de privilegiados. Pero también que hay más valor en el criterio de un profesional de la imagen, el audio o la palabra, cuya vida al fin y al cabo se ha consagrado a estudiar las virtudes y los defectos de su arte. Es ahí donde la apuesta de Magnific cobra sentido: podemos debatir en abstracto sobre los contornos morales del "gusto", pero en última instancia un cliente desea que su marca sea mejor, más vistosa y más impactante que las demás. Y eso no se va a conseguir con slop . Hay un interés mercantil en el criterio. En Xataka La última barrera contra la IA es el buen gusto. El problema es que toda una generación está creciendo sin desarrollarlo Queda pues dirimir la cuestión de los bares y de los restaurantes. Como Cuenca explica, los productos de Magnific están orientados a profesionales que tienen un interés específico en sus herramientas. Serán ellos los que eleven el listón de lo que significa "hecho con IA", apelativo ahora mismo un tanto denostado. Pero no serán ellos quienes nos cambien el aspecto de las calles, de los menús del día y de todos esos comercios que han llenado de slop las ciudades. Todo eso seguramente lo siga haciendo ChatGPT. Quizá llegue un día en el que el gusto se democratice completamente, también en los modelos, y todos podamos adquirirlo de forma inmediata a través de una IA, eliminando el turbulento rastro de carteles clónicos. Magnific se está esforzando, pero ese día aún queda lejos. Imagen | Magnific One En Xataka | La pregunta no es si la IA logrará crear obras de arte. noticias.titulo: La española Magnific lanza One: una IA que toma por ti las decisiones de composición, luz, cámara y estilo
noticias.resumen: Los generadores de imágenes con IA han hecho que crear una escena sea mucho más rápido, pero no necesariamente más sencillo cuando buscamos un resultado concreto. Podemos tener clara la idea y, aun así, dedicar buena parte del trabajo a decidir cómo debe verse, qué óptica utilizaríamos o qué estilo debería dominar la imagen. Es precisamente en esa capa de decisiones donde todavía seguimos interviniendo mucho. Y es también ahí donde Magnific quiere colocar ahora una parte importante de su propuesta. Ahí entra Magnific One , la nueva propuesta de la compañía española. Su funcionamiento, según…
noticias.contenido: Los generadores de imágenes con IA han hecho que crear una escena sea mucho más rápido, pero no necesariamente más sencillo cuando buscamos un resultado concreto. Podemos tener clara la idea y, aun así, dedicar buena parte del trabajo a decidir cómo debe verse, qué óptica utilizaríamos o qué estilo debería dominar la imagen. Es precisamente en esa capa de decisiones donde todavía seguimos interviniendo mucho. Y es también ahí donde Magnific quiere colocar ahora una parte importante de su propuesta. Ahí entra Magnific One , la nueva propuesta de la compañía española. Su funcionamiento, según detalla Magnific, añade un paso previo a la generación: una capa de dirección creativa analiza el prompt, los estilos y las referencias que hayamos proporcionado, desarrolla esas instrucciones y define cómo debería construirse visualmente la imagen. Solo después se produce la generación. En otras palabras, la empresa quiere que podamos expresar la idea sin tener que convertir nosotros mismos cada intención creativa en una larga sucesión de instrucciones técnicas. Una IA que quiere hacer también de director de arte Si bien Magnific presenta One como un "modelo de imagen", la compañía asegura que no ha entrenado un nuevo modelo generativo. Su tecnología propia está en todo lo que rodea a esa generación: el sistema de prompting, la dirección de arte y las reglas que condicionan el resultado antes de producirlo. Debajo sigue funcionando una tecnología de imagen subyacente que puede ir cambiando con el tiempo. One es, por tanto, la capa con la que Magnific pretende mantener una forma de trabajar estable aunque evolucione el motor encargado de crear las imágenes. Detrás de esta arquitectura hay dos problemas que Magnific dice querer resolver. Los modelos de imagen evolucionan rápido y, con cada cambio importante, los equipos pueden verse obligados a reaprender cómo formular prompts o sacar partido a una tecnología nueva. A eso la compañía suma otra preocupación: que buena parte de las imágenes generadas con IA terminan pareciéndose entre sí. One nace como su respuesta a ambas cuestiones: reducir la dependencia del modelo concreto y abrir más caminos visuales a partir de una misma idea. Draft genera cuadrículas de 8 o 16 imágenes antes de llevar una opción a Final | Imagen: Magnific AI El primero de sus dos modos se llama Draft y está pensado para explorar antes de decidir. A partir de un único prompt, el sistema genera una cuadrícula de 8 o 16 imágenes con distintas composiciones, atmósferas y enfoques, todas por el precio de una sola generación. La idea es que podamos comparar varias interpretaciones de una misma propuesta sin tener que lanzar cada opción por separado. Cuando una de ellas se acerca a lo que buscamos, podemos seleccionarla y llevar esa dirección al siguiente paso del proceso. Magnific One separa la exploración rápida en Draft de la generación final en 4K | Imagen: Magnific AI El segundo modo es Final, pensado ya para producir la imagen definitiva. Podemos entrar directamente en él si tenemos clara la dirección que buscamos o llegar desde una propuesta seleccionada previamente en Draft. Magnific permite generar aquí imágenes en 2K o 4K y seguir orientando el resultado mediante estilos y hasta cinco imágenes de referencia. Es el punto en el que la exploración se convierte en una pieza lista para trabajar con mayor calidad, manteniendo todavía margen para decidir qué referencias y lenguaje visual queremos conservar. Magnific convierte las directrices de marca en reglas que guían distintos tipos de contenido | Imagen: Magnific AI Y una imagen unísona para tu marca Brand Kit es la pieza con la que Magnific intenta trasladar esa dirección creativa al terreno de una marca concreta. Podemos alimentarlo con una web, un PDF de identidad, imágenes o una descripción escrita, y un agente extrae elementos como el logotipo, la paleta, la tipografía, el estilo visual y el tono para construir una primera versión dxel kit. Después podemos revisarlo y ajustarlo antes de aplicarlo en Final, donde cada resultado se contrasta con esas reglas para detectar posibles desviaciones en aspectos como la paleta, la tipografía o el logotipo. Para una agencia o un equipo grande, la idea es definir una vez las reglas de cada marca y reutilizarlas después en sus distintos proyectos. Ejemplo de una imagen generada con Magnific One | Imagen: Magnific AI Ese proceso no deja fuera al creativo cuando llega el momento de ajustar los detalles. Magnific incorpora Auto Layers, una función que separa la imagen en capas editables para que podamos modificar elementos concretos sin tener que generarla de nuevo. Desde Designer es posible retocar textos, colores o tipografías, y el trabajo también puede continuar en Figma o Photoshop mediante los plugins de la plataforma. La compañía plantea así One como una herramienta que propone y desarrolla la dirección visual, mientras las decisiones más precisas de acabado siguen quedando en manos del usuario. Magnific One también está pensado para crear imágenes comerciales y de producto | Imagen: Magnific AI Detrás de One está además una compañía española con una historia bastante más larga que la actual ola de IA generativa. La empresa que hoy conocemos como Magnific nació como Freepik en Málaga en 2010 y durante años construyó su negocio alrededor de recursos visuales para creativos. En 2026 adoptó Magnific como nueva identidad para reflejar su transformación hacia una plataforma centrada en herramientas de inteligencia artificial para imagen, vídeo, 3D y audio. Mantiene oficinas en Málaga y San Francisco y asegura contar actualmente con más de un millón de suscriptores de pago . En Xataka Hemos visitado las oficinas de Magnific: hace 15 años vendía fotos de stock, hoy quiere ser el Photoshop de la era de la IA desde Málaga Magnific One está disponible desde el 8 de octubre en todos los planes de pago de la compañía y en todo el mundo, desde la web y sus aplicaciones hasta Spaces y el acceso mediante MCP. Utiliza el sistema de créditos de la plataforma, con las cifras comunicadas por Magnific partiendo de 180 créditos para una generación High en 2K y llegando a 1.000 en Max a 4K. Además, entre el 8 y el 15 de octubre los planes Premium+, Business, Pro Starter y Pro cuentan con generaciones ilimitadas bajo las condiciones de la promoción en la app de escritorio, mientras que Max sigue consumiendo créditos. noticias.titulo: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
noticias.resumen: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

noticias.resumen: Algunos matemáticos están indignados. Otros están preocupados. Y muchos de ellos están fascinados. Todos tienen motivos de peso para sentirse así. noticias.contenido: Algunos matemáticos están indignados. Otros están preocupados. Y muchos de ellos están fascinados. Todos tienen motivos de peso para sentirse así. La irrupción de los modelos de inteligencia artificial (IA) de frontera en el ámbito de la investigación en matemáticas ha desencadenado una catarsis que no es del todo fácil entender. Durante las últimas semanas OpenAI ha protagonizado varios de los grandes hitos de esta década en el terreno de las matemáticas. Y ayer mismo publicó en X un tuit en el que anticipa que está preparando la publicación de más resultados matemáticos producidos por un modelo de frontera interno. Esto no ha hecho más que empezar . A principios de septiembre, uno de los modelos de vanguardia que por el momento solo está siendo utilizado por los investigadores de la propia compañía logró encontrar una solución al problema de Navier-Stokes, uno de los Problemas del Milenio que permanecían sin resolver. Su resultado todavía no ha sido validado de forma independiente por la comunidad matemática, pero desvela algo mucho más profundo: una IA ya es capaz de abordar problemas que durante décadas se les han resistido a los mejores matemáticos del mundo. Tenemos otro ejemplo muy reciente. El pasado 30 de septiembre OpenAI publicó un resultado sobre una versión debilitada de la hipótesis de Riemann. Definitivamente, esto es solo el principio. La comunidad matemática más crítica está horrorizada "OpenAI, que actualmente se defiende en demandas por acusaciones de plagio ilegal , infracción de derechos de autor y dilución de marca, publicó un repositorio de manuscritos que supuestamente contienen soluciones a varios problemas destacados de las matemáticas. Los matemáticos no pidieron que se hiciera este trabajo [...] OpenAI ha demostrado un desprecio total por las normas de la investigación científica, normas que garantizan que las matemáticas sigan siendo fiables, se investiguen de forma ética y sirvan al interés público". En Xataka "El espacio-tiempo podría no ser fundamental": hablamos con Juan Maldacena, el 'Einstein' de nuestra época y claro candidato al Nobel de Física "Publicar más de 700 archivos de golpe no es una demostración de rigor académico, sino una demostración de poder" Este texto es un extracto del comunicado emitido ayer por la Asociación de Matemáticas Humanas como respuesta al lanzamiento de resultados matemáticos de OpenAI del 6 de octubre. Su tono es muy crítico y llega incluso más lejos de lo que cabría esperar: "[...] Instamos a los matemáticos y al público a valorar este modelo de publicación con el debido escepticismo. Publicar más de 700 archivos de golpe no es una demostración de rigor académico, sino una demostración de poder. Instamos a los matemáticos a dejar de colaborar con OpenAI [...]". Es evidente que los ánimos están muy caldeados. Como acabamos de ver, a algunos matemáticos no les hace ninguna gracia que un laboratorio de IA publique de golpe un aluvión de resultados sin someterse a las normas de investigación mayoritariamente aceptadas. En su artículo del 6 de octubre, OpenAI expresa su visión acerca de este asunto: "Para establecer un procedimiento común a la hora de compartir resultados con la comunidad matemática, hemos consultado al Grupo Asesor sobre Matemáticas e Inteligencia Artificial del Instituto de Estudios Avanzados, un organismo independiente, sobre el desarrollo de buenas prácticas. Estamos incorporando sus consejos y recomendaciones públicas a nuestra forma de publicar estos resultados [...]". "Para promover la transparencia y la apertura en la ciencia, también publicamos en el repositorio más detalles sobre cómo obtuvimos los resultados [...] Queremos que estos avances amplíen los límites del conocimiento humano y propicien nuevos progresos en matemáticas [...] Queremos poner capacidades de última generación directamente en manos de los científicos y estamos trabajando para ofrecer de forma responsable el modelo que produjo estos resultados [...]". Hay otro problema de fondo En la comunidad científica existe un consenso casi unánime que defiende que Terence Tao, que tiene la doble nacionalidad australiana y estadounidense, es el auténtico 'Mozart de las matemáticas'. Su prestigio se lo ha ganado a pulso. Ganó la Medalla Fields, que suele ser considerada el Nobel de las matemáticas , en 2006, cuando tenía 31 años. Y se hizo con ella por sus contribuciones en tres áreas fundamentales: la teoría de números, las ecuaciones en derivadas parciales y el análisis armónico. En Xataka 2026 nos ha traído varios prodigios técnicos en componentes de ordenador. También es el año en el que menos usuarios pueden permitírselos Terence Tao es actualmente uno de los mayores impulsores de Lean dentro de la comunidad científica Tao no cree que la IA acabe sustituyendo a los investigadores; sostiene que, en realidad, es una herramienta muy valiosa que permite a los matemáticos dejar atrás la investigación individual y colaborar en proyectos mucho más grandes y ambiciosos. Y predica con el ejemplo . De hecho, ha introducido Lean en su flujo de trabajo diario. Esta herramienta es un asistente de demostraciones y un lenguaje de programación diseñado para verificar los razonamientos matemáticos y comprobar que son totalmente correctos. Tao es actualmente uno de los mayores impulsores de Lean dentro de la comunidad científica. En la coyuntura actual no es razonable acusar a Tao de ser un matemático contrario al uso de la IA. Pese a todo, en su artículo 'Las matemáticas en la era de la IA' ha puesto sobre la mesa con mucha lucidez algunos de los problemas derivados del uso de esta tecnología en el ámbito de la investigación en matemáticas. Una de sus preocupaciones se ciñe a las matemáticas que nos estamos perdiendo al ceder la investigación a un modelo de IA: "Para resolver realmente un problema matemático, proporcionar una mera respuesta (incluso aunque esté formalmente certificada) no es suficiente. Lo que falta es una demostración inteligible que los matemáticos humanos puedan comprender y utilizar para hacer avanzar los objetivos de las matemáticas". Además, Tao considera que aunque un modelo de IA produzca demostraciones correctas y comprensibles, esto no significa que "haya resuelto las matemáticas", como sostienen algunos partidarios de la IA. Según este investigador, las matemáticas no consisten únicamente en resolver problemas, sino también en desarrollar conceptos y teorías, formular nuevas preguntas, unificar áreas diferentes, educar a nuevas generaciones y construir conocimiento acumulativo. noticias.titulo: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
noticias.resumen: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

I love how your films capture what it feels like to be a young girl growing up. We hear so much about the famous men in your family, but how have the successful women in your family inspired and influenced you? Your films capture the experience of what it is to be a young girl in a way words often can’t. CherryEmma That’s nice to hear, thank you. I feel like I got a lot from my mom about being true to yourself, following what you’re interested in and seeing the beauty in your surroundings. My mom always noticed odd details in life, so a lot of my films are made up of those kinds of things. Your films beautifully capture the isolation of hotel rooms – spaces completely detached from a character’s past or future. If you were forced into that stillness and could choose to preserve only one cherished memory while erasing another for ever, what would they be? Malpractice1 It’s hard to pick a memory, but recently we had a party in Versailles for the anniversary of Marie Antoinette and New Order played. When they started playing Ceremony [from the soundtrack] and the lights went on, I just know that in the future when I have to remember a happy memory, that’s going to be it. Even painful memories are part of making you who you are, and you learn from them, so I can’t think of anything I would erase. Continue reading...
